events.title: Jabber (XMPP) first released
events.summary: Jeremie Miller released the first jabberd server on January 4, 1999 — the open-source instant messaging system that became XMPP.
events.about: Jabber used XML streams for federated chat — users on one server could message users on another, unlike closed AOL or MSN networks. The protocols were standardized as XMPP (RFC 6120/6121) and power WhatsApp-era ideas of open messaging. Google Talk, Slack's federation experiments, and Matrix inherit its DNA.

narrative.whyChosen: Jabber was the first widely deployed open, federated instant messaging protocol.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved real-time presence and chat could work across independent servers with open standards.
narrative.problemSolved: Proprietary IM networks trapped users in walled gardens with no interoperability.

events.title: TLS 1.0 standardized
events.summary: RFC 2246 defined TLS 1.0 in January 1999 — the IETF standard that succeeded SSL for encrypted web and application traffic.
events.about: TLS wraps TCP connections with encryption and identity verification — the padlock in your browser, `https://` APIs, and secure database links. Handshakes negotiate ciphers; certificates prove server identity. Every modern site, mobile app backend, and microservice mesh depends on TLS or its successors.

narrative.whyChosen: TLS 1.0 gave the internet a vendor-neutral standard for transport security after proprietary SSL wars.
narrative.whyImportant: It made encrypted HTTP practical at scale and underpins e-commerce and API security today.
narrative.problemSolved: Proprietary SSL implementations fragmented; the web needed one auditable protocol for privacy on the wire.
